causal_claim: Napier's logarithms made cross-entropy loss possible by supplying the logarithm that cross-entropy applies to predicted probabilities.
definition: John Napier published tables of logarithms in Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio in 1614, turning products into sums.
name: Napier's logarithms (1614)

causal_claim: Huygens's mathematical expectation made cross-entropy loss possible by defining the probability-weighted average that cross-entropy computes as an expected log-loss.
definition: Christiaan Huygens published De ratiociniis in aleae ludo in 1657, the first published book on probability, systematising expectation.
name: Huygens's mathematical expectation (1657)

causal_claim: Leibniz's differential calculus made cross-entropy loss possible by providing differentiation for minimising a loss function with respect to model parameters.
definition: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz first published differential calculus in Acta Eruditorum in 1684 in Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis.
name: Leibniz's differential calculus (1684)

causal_claim: Fisher's maximum likelihood made cross-entropy loss possible by showing that fitting a distribution means maximising its likelihood, whose negative logarithm is cross-entropy.
definition: R. A. Fisher introduced the method of maximum likelihood in its modern form in 1922, after first presenting a numerical procedure in 1912.
name: Fisher's maximum likelihood (1922)
source_title: R. A. Fisher and the Making of Maximum Likelihood 1912-1922

causal_claim: Kolmogorov's probability axioms made cross-entropy loss possible by giving predicted and true distributions the rigorous measure-theoretic form cross-entropy compares.
definition: Andrey Kolmogorov axiomatised probability as a normalised measure in Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung in 1933.
name: Kolmogorov's probability axioms (1933)

causal_claim: Mersenne's Académie Parisienne made cross-entropy loss possible by circulating the gambling problems and letters from which probability and expectation emerged.
definition: Marin Mersenne set up the informal Académie Parisienne in 1635, a correspondence network of nearly 140 scholars including Pascal and Fermat.
name: Mersenne's Académie Parisienne (1635)

causal_claim: The Royal Society made cross-entropy loss possible by creating a durable institution that published and arbitrated probability work from Huygens to Bayes and Fisher.
definition: The Royal Society was founded on 28 November 1660 at Gresham College, London, as a college for promoting physico-mathematical experimental learning.
name: The Royal Society (1660)
source_title: Royal Society | British Science, History & Impact | Britannica

causal_claim: Journal des Sçavans made cross-entropy loss possible by inventing the dated scholarly journal through which mathematical results could spread and be cited across Europe.
definition: The Journal des Sçavans, started in France by Denis de Sallo in 1665, was an early learned periodical for diffusing new scholarship.
name: Journal des Sçavans (1665)
source_title: History of publishing - Magazines, Periodicals, Journalism | Britannica

causal_claim: Philosophical Transactions made cross-entropy loss possible by providing the venue that published Halley's life table in 1693 and Bayes's essay in 1763.
definition: Philosophical Transactions first appeared in March 1665 under Henry Oldenburg and is the oldest scientific journal in continuous publication.
name: Philosophical Transactions (1665)
source_title: About | Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A

causal_claim: French Academy of Sciences made cross-entropy loss possible by sustaining the Paris mathematical community that produced Laplace's probability theory and least-squares work.
definition: The Académie des sciences was founded in 1666 by Louis XIV at Jean-Baptiste Colbert's suggestion, holding its first session on 22 December 1666.
name: French Academy of Sciences (1666)

causal_claim: Cardano's Liber de Ludo Aleae made cross-entropy loss possible by importing counting of gambling outcomes into mathematics as the first systematic notion of probability.
definition: Gerolamo Cardano wrote Liber de Ludo Aleae around 1564, defining probability as the ratio of favourable to total possible outcomes for dice games.
name: Cardano's Liber de Ludo Aleae (1564)

causal_claim: Johan de Witt's life annuity valuation made cross-entropy loss possible by transferring expectation from games of chance to pricing real uncertain payments in insurance.
definition: Johan de Witt presented Waerdye van Lyf-renten on 30 July 1671, the first mathematical calculation of the value of life annuities using expected value.
name: Johan de Witt's life annuity valuation (1671)
source_title: The Waerdye - Johan de Witt - The first calculation on the valuation of life annuities

causal_claim: Halley's Breslau life table made cross-entropy loss possible by showing an empirical frequency distribution could represent reality, the target a predicted distribution is later scored against.
definition: Edmond Halley published the first life table computed from statistics, using Breslau births and funerals for 1687-1691, in Philosophical Transactions in 1693.
name: Halley's Breslau life table (1693)
source_title: Catalogue of an Exhibition Illustrating the History of Actuarial Science in the United Kingdom

causal_claim: Gauss's recovery of Ceres made cross-entropy loss possible by proving in astronomy that a probabilistic error model could score competing predictions against observations.
definition: Carl Friedrich Gauss predicted where the lost asteroid Ceres would reappear in December 1801 from Giuseppe Piazzi's few observations, using least squares and an error law later published in 1809.
name: Gauss's recovery of Ceres (1801)
source_title: The Prince of Mathematics | Carl Friedrich Gauss

causal_claim: Boltzmann's entropy formula made cross-entropy loss possible by establishing the logarithmic entropy of a distribution in physics that information theory and cross-entropy later adopted.
definition: Ludwig Boltzmann gave the statistical definition of entropy S = k log W in 1877, linking entropy logarithmically to the number of microstates.
name: Boltzmann's entropy formula (1877)

causal_claim: Graunt's Bills of Mortality frequency counting made cross-entropy loss possible by creating empirical distributions from counted frequencies, the observed distribution cross-entropy is evaluated against.
definition: John Graunt published Natural and Political Observations upon the Bills of Mortality in 1662, deriving a rudimentary life table from burial statistics.
name: Graunt's Bills of Mortality frequency counting (1662)
source_title: Catalogue of an Exhibition Illustrating the History of Actuarial Science in the United Kingdom

causal_claim: Simpson's theory of observational errors made cross-entropy loss possible by first treating measurement error as a probability distribution, a prerequisite for scoring predictions probabilistically.
definition: Thomas Simpson's 1757 memoir laid down that positive and negative errors are equally probable and gave a probability curve for continuous errors of observation.
name: Simpson's theory of observational errors (1757)

causal_claim: Legendre's method of least squares made cross-entropy loss possible by establishing the working pattern of fitting a model by minimising a single scalar loss over data.
definition: Adrien-Marie Legendre published the first clear exposition of the method of least squares in 1805 as an algebraic procedure for fitting equations to data.
name: Legendre's method of least squares (1805)

causal_claim: Laplace's inverse probability made cross-entropy loss possible by practising Bayesian inference that inverts a likelihood, the same likelihood whose log-loss is cross-entropy.
definition: Pierre-Simon Laplace summarised his extension of Bayes's inverse probability in Théorie analytique des probabilités in 1812.
name: Laplace's inverse probability in Théorie analytique des probabilités (1812)

causal_claim: Gibbs's ensemble entropy made cross-entropy loss possible by expressing entropy as an expectation over a probability distribution, the form -sum p log p that cross-entropy generalises.
definition: Josiah Willard Gibbs published Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics in 1902, where the negative average index of probability of an ensemble corresponds to entropy.
name: Gibbs's ensemble entropy (1902)

causal_claim: Pascal-Fermat correspondence made cross-entropy loss possible by founding mathematical probability, without which no predicted distribution could be defined or scored.
definition: Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat corresponded in 1654 on the problem of points, establishing expectation and combinatorial probability.
name: Pascal-Fermat correspondence (1654)
source_title: Probability and statistics | History, Examples, & Facts | Britannica

causal_claim: Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi made cross-entropy loss possible by proving observed frequencies converge to true probabilities, justifying training and scoring distributions on finite samples.
definition: Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi was published posthumously in 1713 and contained the first version of the law of large numbers.
name: Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi (1713)

causal_claim: de Moivre's Doctrine of Chances made cross-entropy loss possible by supplying the binomial distribution and its normal approximation that classifiers later model and score.
definition: Abraham de Moivre published The Doctrine of Chances in 1718, the first textbook on probability theory; its 1738 edition introduced the normal approximation to the binomial.
name: de Moivre's Doctrine of Chances (1718)

causal_claim: Bayes's Essay made cross-entropy loss possible by giving the rule for inverting conditional probabilities, linking observed data to a posterior distribution over hypotheses.
definition: Thomas Bayes's Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances was read at the Royal Society on 23 December 1763 and published in Philosophical Transactions.
name: Bayes's Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763)

causal_claim: Pearson's chi-squared goodness-of-fit test made cross-entropy loss possible by demonstrating a principled scalar measure of mismatch between an expected distribution and observed frequencies.
definition: Karl Pearson published his chi-squared test in 1900, comparing observed frequencies with expected frequencies under a hypothesised distribution.
name: Pearson's chi-squared goodness-of-fit test (1900)
